newsitem.title: JAPAN: Toyota seeks to dampen UK furore over EMU comment.
newsitem.headline: Toyota seeks to dampen UK furore over EMU comment.

text.p: Japanese carmaker Toyota Motor Corp, in an apparent effort to dampen a British pre-election furore sparked by comments by its president, said on Thursday that investment in Britain was still one option in Europe.
But Toyota stuck to its guns in asserting that a single European currency would be a factor in deciding its investment strategy and an advantage for firms operating in Europe.

Thursday's statement came a day after Toyota president Hiroshi Okuda stirred up a row among Britain's ruling Conservatives by seeming to rule out building new factories in the country if it stayed out of Europe's single currency.
Okuda did not deny or retract his earlier remarks in the statement on Thursday.
"Toyota Motor Corporation's position regarding necessary future investment in Europe is now under study and nothing has been decided," he said.
"In the same manner, future investment in the U.K. is being considered as one of many possible options. This policy remains the same and has not changed at all," the statement said.
Okuda also said, however, that EMU (Economic and Monetary Union) was one element in making investment decisions along with location, infrastructure and labour force.
Generally, for companies operating in Europe "a unified currency would reduce currency exchange rate fluctuations and risk and would be a significant advantage," he said.
On Wednesday, Okuda told reporters at a reception that regardless of whether Britain joined the EMU, it might be "excessive" for Toyota to make further investments in that country.
He added that Toyota would shift its European investments to continental Europe if Britain did not join EMU.

Those comments came as an unpleasant shock to the British government. The ruling Conservatives, lagging Labour in the polls before an election which must by held by May 22, have made great play of their ability to attract foreign investment.

The Conservatives are split over the single currency. Prime Minister John Major has been resisting pressure from so-called Eurosceptic lawmakers, who say joining the EMU would end Britain's sovereignty over its own affairs.
But Major last week hardened his earlier line that no decision had been made by saying a Conservative government would be very unlikely to sign up for the first stage of EMU in 1999.

Okuda's comments -- unusual in that Japanese executives often shy away from controversy -- might have been meant to put pressure on Britain to get good investment conditions even if London failed to join the EMU, one analyst said.

"I think Toyota is giving an warning to Britain that it should make more effort to ensure equal investment conditions even if it doesn't join the EMU," said Kazunori Tokuda, a car industry analyst at Wako Research Institute.
Based on cost alone, Britain would still be Toyota's best bet but the firm might consider more output in continental Europe to get closer to consumers, Tokuda added.

Rival carmaker Nissan Motor Co Ltd, meanwhile, said on Thursday that Britain remained an important base for its global strategy and that it had no plans to review its investment strategy because of the single European currency.

"Britain is an important car supply base on the global level. So we have absolutely no intention now to change that status," a Nissan spokeswoman told Reuters. "We are not reviewing our investment strategy now as a result of the Euro (single European currency)."
Honda Motor Co Ltd also echoed that view, telling Reuters it had no plan to change its current output in Britain regardless of the EMU.
